items.bodyEn: Kanaya faced Shimada across the Ōi riverbed, and Hiroshige drew its bank as the far shore of a procession's crossing. In 1870 the new government abolished the carrying system; porters lost their trade almost overnight. Many joined former shogunal retainers who were clearing the Makinohara plateau above the town, and planted the tea fields that cover it today.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō 'Kanaya: Ōigawa Engan'; Makinohara tea histories

items.bodyEn: 相槌, the little はい, ええ and そうですね you drop while someone talks, began at the forge. A swordsmith's apprentice struck the glowing steel in rhythm between the master's blows, hammer answering hammer: 相槌を打つ. A nice coincidence at Kanaya, whose name is written 'metal valley'. Good aizuchi still work that way: keep the beat, never grab the hammer.
items.sourceNote: Daijisen / Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, entry あいづち【相槌】

items.titleEn: When Not to Say んです
items.bodyEn: 〜んです frames a sentence as the explanation behind something both of you can see: 遅れてすみません、電車が止まったんです. Drop it from plain reports and you sound neutral; add it where nothing needs explaining and you sound defensive. 私は学生なんです at a first meeting hints 'so that explains me'. Use it to answer a visible why, and to ask one: どうしたんですか.

渡りに船: you reach the riverbank and a boat is already waiting. The phrase means help that arrives exactly when needed, and dictionaries trace it to a line in the Lotus Sutra about a traveler finding a boat at a ford. On the Ōi, where no boat was allowed, it must have sounded like a dream.
items.sourceNote: Daijisen, entry 渡りに船 (cites the Lotus Sutra phrase 如渡得船)
